{{Short description|Mathematical constant}}
[[File:Fransen-Robinson-Constant-integral.gif|thumb|The curve is {{math|1/&Gamma;(''x'')}}, the shaded region is <math>F = \int_0^a \frac{1}{\Gamma(x)}\,dx</math>. As the upper bound of integration (a) goes to infinity, the approximation above approaches the actual value.]]
The '''Fransén–Robinson constant''', sometimes denoted ''F'', is the [[mathematical constant]] that represents the area between the graph of the [[reciprocal Gamma function]], {{math|1/&Gamma;(''x'')}}, and the positive ''x'' axis. That is,

:<math>F = \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{\Gamma(x)}\,dx = 2.8077702420285...</math>

==Other expressions==
{{unref section |date=May 2024}}
The Fransén–Robinson constant has numerical value {{nowrap|''F'' {{=}} 2.8077702420285...}} <ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Fransén-Robinson Constant |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Fransen-RobinsonConstant.html |access-date=2026-01-11 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>{{OEIS|id=A058655}}, and [[simple continued fraction|continued fraction representation]] [2; 1, 4, 4, 1, 18, 5, 1, 3, 4, 1, 5, 3, 6, ...] {{OEIS|id=A046943}}. The constant is somewhat close to [[e (mathematical constant)|Euler's number]] {{nowrap|''e'' {{=}} 2.71828... .}}  This fact can be explained by approximating the integral by a sum:

:<math>F = \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{\Gamma(x)}\,dx \approx \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{\Gamma(n)} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{n!},</math>

and this sum is the standard series for ''e''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The number e |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/e/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251004184939/https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/HistTopics/e/ |archive-date=2025-10-04 |access-date=2025-11-27 |website=Maths History |language=en-GB |url-status=live }}</ref> The difference is

:<math>F - e = \int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-x}}{\pi^2 + (\ln x)^2}\,dx</math>

or equivalently

:<math>F = e + \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} e^{\pi \tan \theta} e^{-e^{\pi \tan \theta}}\,d\theta.</math>

The Fransén–Robinson constant can also be expressed using the [[Mittag-Leffler function]] as the limit

:<math>F = \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \alpha E_{\alpha, 0}(1).</math>

It is however unknown whether ''F'' can be expressed in [[closed-form expression|closed form]] in terms of other known constants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sampedro |first=Juan Carlos |date=2019-01-17 |title=Some identities involving Inverse Gamma integrals |url=https://login.uml.idm.oclc.org/login?qurl=https://link.springer.com%2farticle%2f10.1007%2fs11139-018-0082-z |journal=The Ramanujan Journal |language=en |volume=48 |issue=3 |pages=577–583 |doi=10.1007/s11139-018-0082-z |issn=1382-4090|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Calculation history==
A fair amount of effort has been made to calculate the numerical value of the Fransén–Robinson constant with high accuracy.

The value was computed to 36&nbsp;decimal places by Herman P. Robinson using 11&nbsp;point [[Newton–Cotes quadrature]], to 65&nbsp;digits by A. Fransén using [[Euler–Maclaurin summation]], and to 80&nbsp;digits by Fransén and S. Wrigge<ref>{{Cite web |title=A058655 - OEIS |url=https://oeis.org/A058655 |access-date=2026-01-11 |website=oeis.org}}</ref> using [[Taylor series]] and other methods. William A. Johnson computed 300&nbsp;digits, and Pascal Sebah was able to compute 1025&nbsp;digits using [[Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature|Clenshaw–Curtis integration]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gourdon |first1=Xavier |last2=Pascal |first2=Sebah |title=Constants and Records of Computation |url=http://numbers.computation.free.fr/Constants/Miscellaneous/Records.html |website=Numbers, constants and computation |access-date=3 July 2022}}</ref>
